evidence: Library of Congress / National Park Service historical interpretation
note: The political project of continental expansion helped create the historical material later mythologized as the American frontier. The Library of Congress explicitly warns that popular images of heroic white settlers and cowboys grew around the settling of the West and shaped later understandings of the frontier.

Rapid territorial acquisition, migration, and state/territorial organization created the political geography in which Nevada's 1860s mining boom and territorial government developed. This is historical context, not a claim that individual miners were personally motivated by Manifest Destiny.
The Civil War halted Mississippi River traffic and ended Clemens's steamboat-pilot career. After a brief Confederate militia stint, he traveled west with his brother to Nevada Territory.
source_label: National Endowment for the Humanities — Documenting Mark Twain

note: Clemens trained as a Mississippi steamboat pilot before the Civil War; the river profession supplied both the pen name 'Mark Twain' and a durable store of language, navigation knowledge, places, and social observation.
source_label: National Endowment for the Humanities — Documenting Mark Twain

note: In Nevada, Clemens tried prospecting and speculative ventures before becoming a reporter for the Virginia City Territorial Enterprise. His western journalism and mining-boom experience were formative to the Mark Twain persona and later writing.
source_label: Library of Congress — Roughing It summary

note: Mark Twain wrote Roughing It, first published in 1872, drawing on his journey and experiences in the Far West.
Roughing It directly narrates Twain's Nevada journey, mining and prospecting episodes, frontier travel, and journalism in the territorial West.
source_label: Library of Congress — Roughing It summary

note: Mark Twain wrote Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.
source_label: National Endowment for the Humanities — Documenting Mark Twain

note: Huckleberry Finn is set in the Mississippi Valley of the 1840s and centers Huck's moral conflict over helping Jim, an enslaved man seeking freedom. Its historical world is antebellum slave society, not the later Civil War itself.
source_label: National Endowment for the Humanities — Documenting Mark Twain

evidence: Library of Congress westward expansion history
note: California's incorporation into the United States, statehood, and subsequent settler migration formed the broader historical setting in which Salinas and other California communities grew during the mid-nineteenth century.

Steinbeck's maternal grandfather Samuel Hamilton was an Irish immigrant and early settler in the Salinas area in the 1850s. That family history gave Steinbeck a direct familial connection to the region's pioneer generation.
source_label: National Steinbeck Center — Steinbeck family stories

note: John Steinbeck wrote East of Eden, published in 1952.
source_label: National Steinbeck Center — John Steinbeck biography

note: East of Eden draws directly on Steinbeck's own Hamilton family history in the Salinas Valley, intertwining those family materials with the fictional Trasks.
source_label: National Steinbeck Center — John Steinbeck biography

note: East of Eden takes its title from Genesis and explicitly reworks the Cain-and-Abel story through Cal and Aron, making the biblical narrative a structural and thematic source rather than a loose comparison.
source_label: Library of Congress — America Reads: East of Eden

evidence: National Steinbeck Center biography and regional archives
note: Steinbeck grew up in Salinas and repeatedly wrote from the agricultural, labor, ecological, and class worlds of the Central Coast. This edge records regional formation rather than claiming a single causal event.
source_label: National Steinbeck Center — John Steinbeck biography

note: John Steinbeck wrote Of Mice and Men, published in 1937.
source_label: Library of Congress — America Reads: Of Mice and Men

note: The novella is set during the Great Depression and follows migrant workers whose hopes for land and security collide with economic precarity.
source_label: Library of Congress — America Reads: Of Mice and Men

note: George and Lennie are itinerant farm laborers who travel to Soledad in Monterey County. The agricultural labor system and regional geography are therefore direct social and geographic context for the novella.
source_label: Library of Congress — Of Mice and Men: Exploring the Context
